title: An Exposition of the Epistle to the Hebrews
author: owen

entries.title: The Brightness of God's Glory Who Purged Our Sins (Hebrews 1:3)
entries.content_summary: Owen opens his exposition on the towering dignity of the Son's person, because the whole weight of the epistle's comfort rests there. The Son is the 'brightness' (effulgence) of the Father's glory and the 'express image' of his very subsistence: not a lesser or derived deity but of one essence with the Father, the eternal radiance shining forth from him. This same Son 'upholds all things by the word of his power' -- a work only God can do, sustaining the whole created order by his mere command. Owen's point is that the one who condescended to 'purge our sins by himself' and then sat down at God's right hand is this infinite person. The efficacy of the priestly work is measured by the majesty of the one who performs it; a divine person gives infinite value to the purgation of sin.
entries.content_detail:
Owen treats verse 3 as the seedbed of the entire epistle. Two phrases fix the Son's deity. 'Brightness of his glory' means the Son is to the Father as the shining radiance is to the light itself -- distinct in person yet inseparable and co-essential, eternally proceeding without division of the divine nature. 'The express image of his person' presses the same truth: the Son is the exact impress or stamp of the Father's subsistence, so that to see him is to see the Father's own glory exhibited. Against every Socinian lowering of Christ, Owen insists these titles ascribe true and proper deity.

To this he joins a work of omnipotence: the Son 'upholds all things by the word of his power.' Owen notes the participle is continuous -- a present, ceaseless sustaining of the universe in being and order, carried not by labour but by a bare word of command. Creation-holding is a divine prerogative; the Son exercises it. Thus the same person who governs all worlds is the one who stooped to the office of a priest.

Owen's pastoral and doctrinal payoff comes in the clause 'when he had by himself purged our sins.' 'By himself' excludes all other means: he was at once the priest and the sacrifice, purging sin by the offering of himself. And because the person offering is the infinite, all-upholding Son, the purgation is of infinite value and full efficacy -- not needing repetition, as the following chapters will argue. The 'sitting down at the right hand of the Majesty on high' is the sign that the work is finished and accepted. Owen thus reads verse 3 as a compressed Christology and soteriology together: the glory of Christ's person is not an abstract speculation but the very ground of the believer's confidence, since so great a person has purged our sins and now reigns.

entries.title: Tasting Death, Destroying the Devil Through Death (Hebrews 2:9, 2:14)
entries.content_summary: Owen expounds the deep necessity and the triumphant end of Christ's humiliation. The Son was 'made a little lower than the angels' precisely 'for the suffering of death' -- his abasement was ordered toward dying. He 'tasted death,' Owen insists, in its full bitterness and curse, not a token but the real thing, and did so 'by the grace of God' for the many sons being brought to glory. Verse 14 gives the strategy: because the children share flesh and blood, the Son took the same nature, so that 'through death' he might destroy the devil, who held the power of death, and free those enslaved by the fear of it. Owen marvels that death is conquered by dying: the Redeemer enters the enemy's own domain and, from within, breaks his tyranny over God's people.
entries.content_detail:
Two things govern Owen's reading. First, the incarnation is purposive. The Son was made 'lower than the angels' not as a bare fact but 'for the suffering of death': his taking of a lower, mortal nature was the necessary means to a death he could not otherwise have died. Owen dwells on 'taste death' -- to taste is to experience really and inwardly; Christ drank death down to its dregs, bearing its penal bitterness as the wages of sin, though for himself he owed nothing. The 'grace of God' is the fountain of the whole transaction, and Owen, a defender of particular redemption, reads the scope in step with the context: the death is 'for' the 'many sons' whom God is 'bringing to glory' in verse 10, the 'brethren' and 'children' God gave him.

Second, verse 14 supplies the divine strategy of redemption. Owen stresses the kinship: 'the children are partakers of flesh and blood,' therefore the Son 'likewise took part of the same.' Only by sharing their nature could he act as their representative and die in their room. The astonishing means is stated as 'through death he might destroy him that had the power of death.' Owen notes the word rendered 'destroy' means to annul, unstring, render powerless -- not to annihilate the devil but to strip him of his usurped dominion. Satan's 'power of death' was the power of accusation and execution over guilty sinners; by satisfying the law and bearing the curse, Christ removes the ground of that power, so death can no longer condemn his people.

Owen's wonder is that the victory is won by submission: the Captain of salvation defeats death by dying, spoiling the strong man in his own house. The fruit is deliverance -- those who 'through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage' are set free, their consciences released from the terror of the grave because the sting of death, which is sin, has been drawn.

entries.title: A Merciful and Faithful High Priest to Make Propitiation (Hebrews 2:17)
entries.content_summary: Here Owen grounds the incarnation in the requirements of the priestly office. It 'behoved' Christ -- there lay a moral necessity -- to be 'made like unto his brethren' in all things, sin excepted, so that he might be a 'merciful and faithful high priest' and 'make reconciliation for the sins of the people.' Owen weighs the two adjectives: 'merciful' looks toward us, a compassion learned by sharing our nature and sufferings; 'faithful' looks toward God, a fidelity in discharging every part of the office committed to him. The end of the priesthood is propitiation -- to expiate sin and turn away wrath. A priest must be taken from among those he represents; therefore the Son truly became man, that a real human high priest might offer a real sacrifice for real sins.
entries.content_detail:
Owen reads 'it behoved him' as marking a necessity arising not from compulsion but from the nature of the office he undertook. A high priest, by the law of the office, must be one with those for whom he acts; he is 'taken from among men' to appear before God on their behalf. Hence the Son was 'in all things' made like his brethren -- sharing a true body and reasonable soul, our infirmities and temptations -- with the single, necessary exception of sin, which Owen guards carefully, for the priest must himself be spotless.

Owen makes much of the paired qualifications. As 'merciful,' Christ is inclined with tender compassion toward the tempted and the guilty; having taken our nature and passed through suffering, his mercy is not abstract but experiential, fitting him to succour those he represents. As 'faithful,' he is entirely trustworthy toward God who appointed him, exact in the whole discharge of his mediation, so that nothing needful to the reconciling of his people is left undone. The one qualification secures our confidence; the other secures the office's integrity.

The office terminates in 'making reconciliation for the sins of the people' -- Owen understands the verb as propitiation: the expiation of sin by sacrifice and thereby the appeasing of the divine displeasure it provoked. This is priestly and sacrificial language: sin is covered or done away by the offering, and God's justice, satisfied, is turned from wrath to favour. Owen is careful that this is 'for the sins of the people' -- a definite people, the 'brethren' and 'children' of the preceding verses -- not an indefinite gesture toward all without exception. The whole verse, then, joins the reality of the incarnation to the necessity of the atonement: because our salvation required a propitiatory sacrifice offered by a genuine and sympathetic human priest, the Son became like us in all things, that he might stand for us in things pertaining to God.

entries.title: Consider the Apostle and High Priest, Greater Than Moses (Hebrews 3:1)
entries.content_summary: Owen turns from the person of Christ to a direct exhortation: 'consider' him. The word bids the mind fix itself attentively on Jesus as the 'Apostle and High Priest of our profession.' Owen sees the two offices as complementary directions of one mediation: as Apostle, Christ is God's supreme envoy sent to us, the final revealer surpassing all prophets; as High Priest, he is our representative sent from us to God. In the verses following, Owen presses the comparison with Moses that governs this section. Moses was faithful, but 'as a servant in the house'; Christ is faithful 'as a Son over his own house,' and so counted worthy of more glory, as the builder has more honour than the house. The Hebrews are urged to prize and hold fast this greater Mediator.
entries.content_detail:
Owen makes the imperative 'consider' the hinge of the passage: it calls for a deliberate, fixed, believing contemplation of Christ, not a passing glance. The readers, 'holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling,' are summoned to turn the whole attention of faith upon Jesus, that they might not drift from him.

Owen finds in the double title a compact statement of Christ's mediatorial work. As 'Apostle,' Christ is the one sent from God to men -- the great ambassador and revealer who declares the mind of God fully and finally, in whom the prophetic line and Moses himself are surpassed, for he speaks not as a servant relaying another's word but as the Son who is himself the Word. As 'High Priest,' he goes the other way, from men to God, to represent his people and present their cause; the offices of revealing and reconciling meet in the single person of Christ Jesus. Under the old economy these were divided -- Moses the lawgiver, Aaron the priest; in Christ they are united.

The comparison with Moses, which Owen expounds at length from the following verses, is the point of the exhortation. Moses was indeed 'faithful in all his house,' and Owen will not diminish that honour; but he was faithful 'as a servant,' and his faithfulness had the character of testimony to things that were to be spoken after -- it pointed forward. Christ is faithful 'as a Son over his own house,' the house being the church, which is his by right of building and ownership. As the one who built the house has more honour than the house, so Christ is counted worthy of more glory than Moses. Owen's pastoral aim is plain: since the Mediator now set before them so far exceeds the greatest servant of the old covenant, the Hebrews have every reason to hold their profession fast and none to fall back to the shadows Moses served.

entries.title: There Remains a Sabbath Rest for the People of God (Hebrews 4:9)
entries.content_summary: On the promise that 'there remaineth a rest to the people of God,' Owen builds his great meditation on gospel rest. He distinguishes several rests in Scripture: God's own rest after creation, sealed in the Sabbath; the rest of Canaan into which Joshua led Israel; and a further, better rest that still 'remains.' Owen's argument, drawn from Psalm 95, is that if the Canaan rest had been the final one, David would not, long afterward, still speak of a rest to be entered 'today.' Therefore a Sabbath-keeping abides for God's people: the spiritual rest found now in Christ by faith, in which we cease from our own works as God did from his, and the consummate rest of glory to come. Faith is the way in; unbelief shuts men out.
entries.content_detail:
Owen's exposition of this verse anchors one of his longest discussions, on the nature and perpetuity of a day of rest. The reasoning is exegetical. The writer to the Hebrews argues from Psalm 95, where God, speaking through David, still warns a later generation not to harden their hearts lest they fail to 'enter into my rest.' Owen presses the chronology: Israel under Joshua had already entered Canaan; yet centuries afterward God still holds out a rest to be entered 'today.' It follows that the Canaan rest, real as it was, was typical and not final; a greater rest was still in prospect. Hence 'there remaineth a rest' -- Owen notes the distinctive word chosen here, a Sabbath-keeping or Sabbath-rest, which links this remaining rest to God's own primeval rest.

Owen unfolds the rest in stages. There is God's rest at creation, when he ceased from his works and blessed the seventh day. There is the rest of the land, a shadow. And there is the gospel rest -- the rest of the soul that comes to Christ and finds relief from the burden of sin and the toil of self-justification. Verse 10 gives its inward character: 'he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his.' Owen reads this as ceasing from all confidence in one's own works for acceptance, resting instead upon the finished work of Christ -- the very posture of justifying faith.

This rest has a present and a future dimension. Believers enter it now, by faith, in peace of conscience and communion with God; they enter it fully hereafter, in the eternal rest of glory. Correspondingly, Owen argues from the passage that a stated day of rest continues under the gospel, now transferred to the Lord's Day, the first day, commemorating the finished work of the risen Christ. Throughout, the warning stands as the counterpart of the promise: it is unbelief, and the hardening of heart it breeds, that shuts men out of God's rest, and faith alone that enters in.

entries.title: The Sympathizing High Priest and the Throne of Grace (Hebrews 4:15, 4:16)
entries.content_summary: Owen draws the epistle's practical centre out of these verses: because our high priest can be 'touched with the feeling of our infirmities,' believers may 'come boldly unto the throne of grace.' Christ was 'in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin,' and from that real experience there springs a genuine, tender fellow-feeling for the tempted and afflicted. This sympathy, Owen stresses, is no mere pity from a distance but the compassion of one who has himself passed through our trials. It is the ground of the exhortation that follows. The mercy-seat has become for us a 'throne of grace,' and to it we are invited to draw near with confidence -- not presumption -- to 'obtain mercy' for our guilt and 'find grace to help' in every season of need.
entries.content_detail:
Owen treats these two verses as promise and inference. The promise is the sympathy of Christ: 'we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities.' The double negative, Owen observes, is emphatic -- far from being unable to sympathize, our priest is fully able and ready. The ground is his own experience: he 'was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.' Owen is careful with the exception. Christ knew temptation from without -- hunger, weariness, grief, Satan's assaults, the pressures that beset our nature -- and felt their force truly; but there was in him no inward corruption, no consenting to sin, for temptation found nothing in him. His sinlessness does not lessen his sympathy but perfects it, for sin in us dulls compassion, while his unstained nature feels our sorrows purely.

Owen distinguishes this compassion from mere divine pity. As God, the Son always regarded his people; but by taking our nature and suffering in it, he acquired an experiential, human fellow-feeling, so that he is inwardly moved toward the tempted as one who has been there. This is a spring of unspeakable comfort to weak and assaulted believers.

From this Owen draws the exhortation of verse 16: 'Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace.' The 'therefore' rests the whole invitation on the priest's sympathy. Owen notes that what was the 'mercy-seat' -- the place of atonement, once approached only by the high priest, once a year, with blood -- is now for believers a 'throne of grace,' freely open. 'Boldly' means with holy freedom and confidence of acceptance, the opposite of the bondage and terror of the old approach, yet never with irreverence. The double aim answers our double need: 'mercy' for the guilt of sins past, and 'grace to help in time of need' -- seasonable, sufficient supply for present weakness and future trial. Assurance, for Owen, is thus not a feeling worked up in us but a confidence grounded in the person and office of our sympathizing priest.

entries.title: A Priest Forever After Melchizedek, Saving to the Uttermost (Hebrews 5:6, 7:17, 7:25)
entries.content_summary: Owen gathers the argument of the middle chapters: Christ is 'a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek,' and therefore 'able to save to the uttermost.' The Melchizedek order, Owen shows, is superior to the Aaronic -- royal as well as priestly, without recorded beginning or succession, and established by God's own oath. Above all it is unchangeable and everlasting: this priest does not die and hand on his office, but 'ever liveth.' From that perpetuity Owen draws the great conclusion of 7:25. Because Christ continues a priest forever, he can save 'to the uttermost' -- completely and to the very end -- all who come to God by him, for he 'ever liveth to make intercession for them.' His endless life guarantees the finishing of their salvation; the priest who never dies cannot fail those he represents.
entries.content_detail:
Owen reads Psalm 110:4, cited at 5:6 and again at 7:17, as the divine charter of Christ's priesthood: 'Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.' Two things follow. First, Christ's priesthood is not of the order of Aaron but of Melchizedek, and Owen expounds from chapter 7 the marks of its superiority. Melchizedek was king as well as priest -- king of righteousness and of peace -- uniting the two offices that Aaron never held; he appears in the record without genealogy, 'without father, without mother,' without registered beginning or end of days, so that he stands as a type of a priesthood that does not depend on descent or succession; and Abraham, with Levi in his loins, paid tithes to him and was blessed by him, the lesser by the greater. Second, this priesthood is confirmed by an oath of God, where the Levitical was not, marking it as unchangeable and the covenant it serves as better.

The crown of the argument, for Owen, is the perpetuity stated in 7:24-25: 'he continueth ever' and has 'an unchangeable priesthood.' Because he does not die and pass the office to another, but abides a living priest forever, his saving work is never interrupted or left unfinished. Hence the conclusion: 'he is able to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him.' Owen unpacks 'to the uttermost' as completeness both in extent and in duration -- a full salvation carried through to its very end, lacking nothing and failing at no point.

The ground is his unceasing intercession: 'seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.' Owen understands Christ's heavenly intercession not as fresh suffering or repeated sacrifice, but as the continual, authoritative presentation of himself and his once-offered sacrifice before the Father, pleading its virtue for his people and securing the application of all its benefits. Because this living advocacy never ceases, the perseverance and final salvation of those who come to God by Christ is made certain. The endlessness of the priest is the guarantee of the endlessness of the salvation.

entries.title: The Warning Against Apostasy and the Perseverance of the Saints (Hebrews 6:4, 6:6)
entries.content_summary: Owen handles the sternest of the warning passages with characteristic care. The people described are 'once enlightened,' having 'tasted the heavenly gift' and been made 'partakers of the Holy Ghost,' yet if they 'fall away' it is 'impossible' to renew them to repentance. Owen argues that these are common, not saving, operations of the Spirit -- illumination, gifts, and experiences that may be had short of justifying faith and true union with Christ. The apostasy in view is total, deliberate, and malicious: a renouncing of Christ that 'crucifies him afresh.' It is irremediable, not because grace runs short, but because such apostates reject the only remedy. Owen insists this does not overthrow the perseverance of true saints, who are kept by God and never so finally fall; the passage describes hypocrites and temporary believers, not the regenerate elect.
entries.content_detail:
Owen's exposition here is a model of careful distinction, for the passage has long troubled those who hold the perseverance of the saints. He fixes first on the description of the persons. They were 'enlightened' -- granted a real illumination of the mind in the knowledge of gospel truth. They 'tasted of the heavenly gift' and 'the good word of God' and 'the powers of the world to come' -- they had genuine, affecting experiences of gospel realities and perhaps of miraculous gifts. They were 'made partakers of the Holy Ghost' -- sharers, Owen argues, in the Spirit's common gifts and operations. But Owen presses the point that nothing here names the saving graces: justifying faith, adoption, union with Christ, sanctifying renewal, the love of God shed abroad in the heart. All that is said may be found in men who are enlightened and gifted yet never truly regenerate -- the stony-ground hearers who receive the word with joy but have no root.

On this basis Owen reads the 'falling away' as the total and final apostasy of such persons: not a lapse into sin from which believers may be recovered, but a deliberate, wilful, and malicious renunciation of the gospel once professed, against knowledge and conviction. Verse 6 gives its character -- they 'crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame,' taking their old place among Christ's crucifiers.

The 'impossibility' of renewing them, Owen argues, lies not in any deficiency of God's power or grace but in the nature of their sin: having knowingly cast off the only sacrifice for sin, they leave themselves no remedy, for there remains no other Christ to be preached to them. Owen is emphatic that this in no way endangers the true believer. The elect, born of God and united to Christ, are kept by his power and preserved by his unfailing intercession; they may fall grievously, but not totally and finally. The warning is real, and is one of the means God uses to preserve his own, but the apostates it describes were never savingly Christ's.

entries.title: Mediator of a Better Covenant on Better Promises (Hebrews 8:6, 8:10)
entries.content_summary: On these verses Owen sets out his covenant theology. Christ has obtained a 'more excellent ministry' because he is 'the mediator of a better covenant, established upon better promises.' The new covenant is better than the old (Sinai) both in its mediator and in what it secures. Owen highlights the promises quoted from Jeremiah: God will 'put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts,' will be their God, and 'their sins and iniquities will I remember no more.' These are promises of efficacious grace -- inward renewal, saving knowledge of God, and free and final forgiveness -- not merely of an outward, conditional arrangement. Where the old covenant demanded and could not give, the new covenant bestows what it requires. Its blessings are secured in Christ's blood and infallibly applied to all its members.
entries.content_detail:
Owen reads 8:6 as the transition from the priesthood to the covenant it administers. Christ's ministry is 'more excellent' in exact proportion as the covenant he mediates is better than the old; the dignity of the mediator and the excellency of the covenant rise and fall together. Owen takes the 'better covenant' to be the new covenant, formally established and confirmed in the blood of Christ, over against the covenant God made with Israel at Sinai, which is now removed as 'old' and 'ready to vanish away.'

The superiority lies chiefly in the 'better promises' on which the new covenant is 'established' -- Owen notes the word means enacted as a law, given the force of a settled constitution. He expounds the promises cited from Jeremiah 31. First, 'I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts' -- an internal, effectual work of regeneration and sanctification, whereby God gives the obedience the law demands, writing his will upon the renewed heart instead of only upon tables of stone. Second, 'I will be to them a God, and they shall be to me a people' -- the covenant bond of communion, God giving himself as the portion of his people. Third, all shall 'know the Lord, from the least to the greatest' -- a saving, experiential knowledge diffused among all covenant members. Fourth, 'their sins and iniquities will I remember no more' -- full, free, and final forgiveness, grounded in the one sacrifice of Christ.

Owen's decisive point is that these are promises of grace that God himself works, not conditions left to human strength. The old covenant at Sinai demanded righteousness but did not communicate the power to perform it, and so, considered as a covenant of works for life, it left its subjects under its curse. The new covenant is unilateral in its efficacy: God undertakes to do in his people what he requires of them. Therefore its blessings are not merely offered but infallibly conveyed to those it embraces, for the same blood that ratifies the covenant secures the application of all its promises.

entries.title: Eternal Redemption by His Own Blood, One Offering Perfecting Forever (Hebrews 9:12, 9:14, 10:10, 10:14)
entries.content_summary: Owen brings together the heart of Christ's priestly work: by his own blood he 'entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption,' and 'by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.' Owen weighs the contrasts. Not the blood of goats and calves but his own blood; not the earthly sanctuary but heaven itself; not yearly repetition but 'once' for all. Because the sacrifice is of infinite worth, its redemption is 'eternal' -- accomplished, not merely offered, and never to be repeated. Verse 9:14 adds that Christ 'through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot,' and that his blood 'purges the conscience from dead works,' reaching the inward guilt the old rites never touched. And its effect is final: the one offering has 'perfected for ever' those it sanctifies, leaving no more offering for sin.
entries.content_detail:
Owen expounds the sacrifice of Christ under the two great emphases of these chapters: its efficacy and its finality. From 9:12 he draws the contrast between type and reality. The Levitical high priest entered the earthly holy place year by year with the blood of animals; Christ entered 'the holy place' -- heaven itself, the true sanctuary -- 'by his own blood,' and 'once.' The single entrance corresponds to a single, all-sufficient sacrifice. And the fruit is stated as accomplished, not merely attempted: 'having obtained eternal redemption for us.' Owen stresses the verb -- Christ found and procured redemption as a thing actually secured, and it is 'eternal' both because its price is of infinite value and because its effect abides forever, needing no repetition.

Verse 9:14 carries the argument inward. Christ 'through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God' -- the offering was voluntary, of his whole spotless person, sustained by his own divine Spirit, and directed Godward as a true sacrifice. Its effect answers the deepest need: his blood 'purges the conscience from dead works to serve the living God.' Owen observes that the ceremonial sacrifices could cleanse only outwardly, sanctifying to the purifying of the flesh; the blood of Christ reaches the conscience itself, removing the real guilt of sin that no legal rite could take away, and freeing the worshipper for living service.

From chapter 10 Owen presses the finality. 'By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all' (10:10): the single offering, done according to the Father's will, sets his people apart as holy to God. 'By one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified' (10:14): Owen reads 'perfected for ever' as a completed and permanent perfection -- a full expiation and acceptance that cannot be added to or repeated, so that, as verse 18 concludes, 'there is no more offering for sin.' The very singleness of the sacrifice is Owen's proof of its perfection, for what is repeated confesses itself insufficient. And 'them that are sanctified' marks the definite compass of its effect: the offering actually perfects a particular people, securing their standing before God once and for all.

entries.title: Looking to Jesus, the Author and Finisher of Faith (Hebrews 12:2)
entries.content_summary: Owen closes the running theme of faith and perseverance with the command to look 'unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith.' The word means to look away -- from every distraction, weight, and fear -- and to fix the eye of faith on Christ alone. He is faith's 'author,' the one who begins it in us and ran its course perfectly before us, and its 'finisher,' who carries it through to completion. Owen sets before believers his pattern: 'for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, despising the shame,' and is now 'set down at the right hand of the throne of God.' The exalted, once-suffering Christ is thus both the object that draws faith and the example that sustains it, so that weary believers may run their race with endurance.
entries.content_detail:
Owen reads this verse as the climax of the exhortation begun with the cloud of witnesses: having named the saints who lived by faith, the writer now directs the eye to the one supreme example and object, Jesus himself. The participle 'looking' means, Owen notes, a looking away -- turning the eye off from all other things, the weights and the besetting sin, the discouragements and the fear of suffering, in order to fix it steadily upon Christ. This fixed regard of faith is the secret of endurance.

Owen weighs the double title. Christ is the 'author' of faith -- its beginner and leader, the one who both works faith in his people by his Spirit and himself went before them as the great pattern of a believing life, the captain who leads the way. He is also its 'finisher' -- the one who perfects and consummates what he begins, carrying his people's faith through to its appointed end, so that the grace he authors he also completes. Faith thus depends on Christ from first to last.

The pattern Owen holds up is Christ's own endurance: 'for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, despising the shame.' The joy set before him -- his glory and the salvation of his people -- sustained him through the utmost suffering and disgrace, which he despised, counting the shame as nothing beside the end in view. And the outcome is his session: he 'is set down at the right hand of the throne of God,' the reward of his endurance and the pledge of his people's. Owen's application is direct. Believers, wearied in the race and tempted by present affliction, are to consider him -- how he suffered and where he now sits -- that they may 'not be wearied and faint in their minds,' but run with patience, assured that the one who authored their faith will also finish it.
